Documentation / Developer / 2D viewport navigation and rendering performance

2D viewport navigation and rendering performance

The investigation started from 012a2ad9 (version 1.7.31). The published change builds on 20355ec9 (version 1.7.49), after the unified typography merge and the vertical pan fix. Fixture labels use the same font catalog, shaped glyphs and text commands in the interactive viewer, Layout editor and document capture.

Confirmed causes

  • Pan motion wrote five saved viewport values through ConfigManager::SetFloat. Wheel and keyboard navigation took the same write path. A changed value incremented the project render revision. On the next lightweight controller poll, a new render revision invalidated visibility candidates and scheduled resource synchronization. Settling the interaction could also schedule an unconditional controller update.
  • The composed fixture label cache cleared on a new render revision or a change to the serialized fixture-label overrides. A camera change consequently caused all eligible labels to be composed again. Editing one fixture's style also discarded warm entries for other fixtures.
  • The composed-label path received no interactive-mode policy. It visited all visible-layer fixtures and issued two projections per glyph before accounting for the viewport.
  • Before the typography merge, the legacy renderer submitted one NanoVG frame per fixture stack and repeated its text measurements. After the merge, legacy fixture settings use canonical composition. The renderer was still resolving stack baselines and font line metrics on cache hits.

Camera and label changes

Live pan offsets and zoom stay on the panel. A drag persists the final position on button release or capture loss. Wheel and keyboard changes persist when input settles. The active project's save and dirty-prompt paths flush pending navigation, and Fit to Scene persists immediately. Existing saved keys, value normalization and project dirty tracking still apply. The camera, view orientation and 2D render mode keys advance the presentation revision alone.

Pan uses the live physical pointer inside the canvas with the event position as a fallback outside it. The final drag sample comes from the release event. Camera movement invalidates pointer hit results and placement alignment. During a temporary pan, clipboard placement realigns once after navigation instead of moving the scene object on camera paints. The existing wxWidgets redraw queue still coalesces input.

The composition cache retains entries by fixture UUID and compares label values, view orientation, projected anchor bounds, and the resolved field styles. A scene revision triggers pruning of deleted UUIDs. A new override document supplies resolved style inputs for each entry at lookup. Changing one fixture or field leaves unrelated cache entries warm. An anchor change recomposes the fixture only if it changes the bounds used to place the text. A new font catalog invalidates compositions. The typography layer shares glyph contours across fixtures. A warm cache hit skips stack positioning, font line metrics and shaping. Pan and zoom only change the mapping of those commands to framebuffer pixels.

The screen pass tests the composed field's text envelope, including font bearings, accents, the screen-space outline and rasterizer padding. The test uses the label's bounds even if its fixture is outside the viewport. It keeps the whole field when its envelope touches an edge. The projection retains Bottom's reversed anchor axis and the existing unmirrored glyphs. The renderer projects each surviving glyph once, reuses NanoVG font IDs and keeps the outline-then-fill order, including the shared typography raster path and vector glyph fallback. Document capture takes the full path and retains offscreen text commands for the document renderer to clip or place.

2D and 3D pipeline differences

Both viewports use the shared resource controller, bounds cache, and visible set. 3D also pumps progressive resource work independently of paint and can resume a pending cursor when movement settles. 2D services pending work from paint, defers it during interaction, and drains it for capture. After the camera fix, movement alone no longer starts a resource generation or dirties the scene's depth-sorted lists. A new 2D orientation still requires an orientation-specific depth order. A changed camera can still require a new frustum-visible set for trusses and scene objects. Fixtures remain candidates for geometry because resource bounds can be conservative or incomplete.

The 3D renderer also has adaptive mesh representations and optional moving frame work, including outline deferral. 2D intentionally takes the authored mesh path where a symbol is unavailable. Its mesh edges can affect the orthographic profile, picking and document output. Measure that path with mesh-heavy scenes before changing it. If it dominates, a candidate is a cached, screen-only orthographic edge representation keyed by source mesh revision, orientation, relevant instance transform and physical pixel scale. Retain silhouette and hard edges, admit it only within a measured framebuffer error tolerance, and use authored data for capture and picking. The current renderer uses authored geometry for these paths.

The remaining work to measure includes the fixture scan and style-key lookups, frustum testing under pan, geometry and outline submission on mesh-heavy scenes, and ruler, grid, support labels and hover. Cold label composition still runs for offscreen fields whose ink envelope is unknown. The renderer still submits individual NanoVG glyph draws after culling. A spatial index or glyph batching change would need separate profiling and edge and outline comparisons.

Repeatable benchmark

  1. Build the original and corrected revisions with the same build type and dependencies. Start both with the same preferences, renderer, display scale, viewport dimensions and VSync setting. Use separate runs for 2D and 3D to isolate each viewport’s swaps.
  2. Use two saved copies of representative MVR scenes. Use a small plot with about 25 fixtures and a mixed large plot with 500–1,000 fixtures, trusses and authored mesh objects. Keep the same project and resource files between revisions. Record the fixture count, approximate mesh complexity, number of styled labels and resolved GDTF resources. Include names, fixture IDs and DMX addresses. Save a second configuration for a geometry-heavy run where the render mode draws detailed meshes.
  3. Warm the project until resource loading completes and labels have been drawn. Run 30 seconds of middle-button back-and-forth pan, then 30 seconds of alternating wheel zoom at the same starting scale. Use the same pointer path and event timing on both builds. Include a path that moves most labels outside the view. Repeat each run three times. Record cold startup and settle frames separately. For the 3D reference use the same scene, an orthographic view when available and a comparable visible area.
  4. Diagnostics are off by default. Set PERASTAGE_VIEWER2D_PERF=1 before launching the corrected build. The application writes one Viewer2D performance report per 120 presented frames and a final partial batch on a normal close. Each report includes mean, nearest-rank p95, p99 and maximum frame times with and without swap. Input-to-swap measures the oldest camera update included in each presented frame up to return from the buffer swap. Display scanout and compositor latency require external measurement. Stage timings are counts and CPU-side milliseconds, and nested stages overlap. Glyph counts describe submitted fixture-label ink. All timer samples come from the CPU side.
  5. Compare both builds and the 3D reference with the same OpenGL swap trace or external frame-time recorder. Use its per-frame samples to compute the run mean, p95 and maximum. Keep CPU submission times, swap intervals and end-to-end display metrics in separate columns. When comparing the corrected build's application logs, combine batch means by sample count and retain the largest maximum. Keep p95/p99 per batch unless the tool also captured individual frame samples. Avoid hardware-dependent CI gates.
  6. Check the corrected run's warm pan and zoom batches for zero composed label rebuilds, scene invalidations, resource syncs or re-sorts caused by camera input. Move and rename a fixture and change one field's typography. Its composition should rebuild with a matching cause. Pan offscreen and back and compare the culled and submitted label/glyph counts. Repeat with grid and ruler off to isolate their contribution.

Linux Debug benchmark on the 1.7.31 base

These single-run software OpenGL measurements, from Xvfb and Mesa llvmpipe, compare the original 1.7.31 checkout with the first implementation before integration with unified typography. Both builds opened the same saved projects, with 24 or 600 fixtures using the bundled Dummy 1ch GDTF. The projects use styled names with accented characters, IDs, DMX addresses and outlines. The framebuffer was 586 × 582 pixels. A physical middle-button pan ran for 18 seconds at 30 pointer samples per second. The trace measures time between entry into consecutive glXSwapBuffers calls for the viewport, excluding the first two seconds of the gesture. These figures describe repaint cadence on this software-rendering setup.

Styled fixtures Build Intervals Mean (ms) p95 (ms) Worst (ms)
24 Baseline 306 51.9 91.7 190.6
24 Corrected 465 34.2 42.3 128.4
600 Baseline 23 685.5 781.5 825.7
600 Corrected 102 154.6 199.2 218.4

The 3D perspective reference used the same 600-fixture scene. Across 911 swap intervals, the mean was 17.5 ms, p95 was 22.8 ms and the worst interval was 102.3 ms. This reference used 3D's own camera, canvas size and hover-label path.

For the 600-fixture project, the first corrected 120-frame diagnostics batch recorded 600 compositions, each a cold entry, and 59,349 offscreen label rejections. Label submission and flushing took 16.7 seconds in that batch, compared with 2.2 seconds for the scene. The warm 24-fixture batches recorded no composition rebuilds, resource syncs or re-sorts. After startup, the resting 2D viewport crops matched pixel for pixel in the sampled, downscaled screenshots from both project sizes.

On the 1.7.31 base, the Linux Debug application built successfully and 41 focused CTest cases passed, including the saved-project round trip, label composition and culling, viewport coordinate math, drag and placement policy, shared typography, and PDF serialization. Translation and repository guardrails passed. The live Print Viewer 2D action generated a readable A3 PDF of the 24-fixture project with visible names, IDs and DMX addresses. Native Windows and macOS runs, hardware OpenGL measurements, and full visual parity across the Layout editor, SVG and PDF remain to be verified.

Visual and interaction checks

  • Pan and zoom in Top, Front and Side, and in Bottom where supported. Reopen the saved project and verify the last position and zoom. Keep long and accented labels with thick outlines just inside each edge, including a text field offset into the viewport from a fixture outside it.
  • Select an object after panning with the pointer stationary. Drag fixtures, try constrained and snapped movement, and check hover on fixtures, trusses and objects. Start single and batch clipboard placement, pan temporarily with the left or middle button, then resume snapping and confirm or cancel.
  • Compare the editor, Layout viewport, 2D SVG and PDF with identical label settings and paper bounds. Include mixed legacy and composed fields and both regular and bold text. Exercise the capture while a navigation interaction is pending.
  • Run the Debug tests on Windows, Linux and macOS. Test on at least one high-DPI display and with fractional scaling where the platform offers it.
